---
title: "High dimensions"
subtitle: "ConvolutionInterpolations.jl against Interpolations.jl on grids of two to five dimensions"
engine: julia
---

Interpolation on tensor-product grids as the number of dimensions grows: the convolution
kernels against the linear and cubic B-spline interpolants of Interpolations.jl, the one other
package that interpolates on grids in any dimension. A separable kernel of width $w$ per axis
touches $w^N$ grid values per evaluation, so the cost of a wide kernel grows fast with the
dimension while its accuracy does not: this page measures both. First the cost and the
accuracy of every method at the same per-axis resolution from two to five dimensions, then
convergence and time to accuracy in three dimensions, and finally lazy construction, which
is what makes large grids in many dimensions affordable to build at all.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Packages, the methods and the test function"
using ConvolutionInterpolations
import Interpolations
using Chairmarks, Printf, Random, CairoMakie

# the test function: the N-dimensional Runge function with a mild parameter, non-separable and
# smooth on [-1, 1]^N, so that the coarse grids a high-dimensional study can afford resolve it
f(x...) = 1 / (1 + sum(abs2, x))

# the grid: n knots per axis on [-1, 1], in N dimensions, and the values on it
axes_nd(N, n) = ntuple(_ -> range(-1.0, 1.0, length = n), N)
values_nd(N, n) = [f(x...) for x in Iterators.product(axes_nd(N, n)...)]

# each method maps the axes and the values to a callable interpolant of N arguments; the
# stencil width per axis is what the cost per evaluation grows with, as width^N
methods_nd = [
    "Interpolations.jl linear" => (ax, v) -> Interpolations.scale(Interpolations.interpolate(v, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Linear())), ax...),
    "Interpolations.jl cubic"  => (ax, v) -> Interpolations.scale(Interpolations.interpolate(v, Interpolations.BSpline(Interpolations.Cubic(Interpolations.Line(Interpolations.OnGrid())))), ax...),
    "ConvInterp :a3"           => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :a3),
    "ConvInterp :a4"           => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :a4),
    "ConvInterp :b5"           => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :b5),
    "ConvInterp :b7"           => (ax, v) -> convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :b7),
]
width = Dict("Interpolations.jl linear" => 2, "Interpolations.jl cubic" => 4, "ConvInterp :a3" => 4,
             "ConvInterp :a4" => 6, "ConvInterp :b5" => 10, "ConvInterp :b7" => 12)

# m random test points inside the grid, as an N × m matrix, and the exact values there; the
# points stay two percent clear of the boundary, so that the methods' different boundary rules
# do not decide the error
function testpoints(N, m)
    P = 0.98 .* (2 .* rand(MersenneTwister(1), N, m) .- 1)
    (P = P, exact = [f(p...) for p in eachcol(P)])
end

# evaluate an interpolant at every column of P
evalpts(itp, P) = [itp(p...) for p in eachcol(P)]

fmt(t) = t < 1e-6 ? @sprintf("%.0f ns", 1e9 * t) : t < 1e-3 ? @sprintf("%.1f μs", 1e6 * t) :
         t < 1 ? @sprintf("%.2f ms", 1e3 * t) : @sprintf("%.2f s", t);
```

## Cost and accuracy against dimension

Sixteen knots per axis, from two dimensions (256 grid values) to five (a million), every
method built on the same grids and evaluated at ten thousand random points. The time to
construct, the time per evaluation, and the largest error against the function.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The dimension study"
Ns = 2:5
n_axis = 16
m_test = 10_000
res = Dict()                                              # (name, N) => (setup, query per point, error)
for N in Ns
    ax = axes_nd(N, n_axis); v = values_nd(N, n_axis)
    tp = testpoints(N, m_test)
    for (name, m) in methods_nd
        itp = m(ax, v)
        res[(name, N)] = (setup = (@b $m($ax, $v)).time,
                          query = (@b evalpts($itp, $(tp.P))).time / m_test,
                          err   = maximum(abs.(evalpts(itp, tp.P) .- tp.exact)))
    end
end

fig = Figure(size = (800, 440))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; yscale = log10, xlabel = "dimension", ylabel = "time per evaluation [s]", xticks = Ns)
for (name, _) in methods_nd
    scatterlines!(ax1, Ns, [res[(name, N)].query for N in Ns]; markersize = 8, label = name)
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax1)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| time per evaluation | stencil | ", join(("$(N)D" for N in Ns), " | "), " |")
println("|:--|--:|", "--:|"^length(Ns))
for (name, _) in methods_nd
    println("| ", name, " | ", width[name], "ᴺ | ", join((fmt(res[(name, N)].query) for N in Ns), " | "), " |")
end
println()
println("| construction | ", join(("$(N)D" for N in Ns), " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(Ns))
for (name, _) in methods_nd
    println("| ", name, " | ", join((fmt(res[(name, N)].setup) for N in Ns), " | "), " |")
end
println()
println("| largest error | ", join(("$(N)D" for N in Ns), " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(Ns))
for (name, _) in methods_nd
    println("| ", name, " | ", join((@sprintf("%.1e", res[(name, N)].err) for N in Ns), " | "), " |")
end
```

In two and three dimensions every method evaluates in a few hundred nanoseconds and the
stencil hardly matters. From four dimensions it decides everything: the cost per evaluation
follows the stencil's $w^N$, so the wide kernels fall two orders of magnitude behind the cubic
B-spline in five dimensions, and `:a3`, which has the cubic's stencil, evaluates somewhat
slower than it. The accuracy, by contrast, does not depend on the dimension at all: a tensor
product keeps each axis's order, so at a fixed per-axis resolution each method's error is the
same number from two dimensions to five, and the order shows as the ratio between the rows —
`:b7` two orders of magnitude below the cubic, `:a4` one, `:a3` level with it. Which is the
trade of the page: in many dimensions, order costs $w^N$ per point and buys the same accuracy
it buys in one — which is why the default kernel narrows with the dimension, from `:b7` in
one and two dimensions to `:b5` in three and `:a4` in four and five.

## Convergence and time to accuracy in three dimensions

Three dimensions, from 11 to 81 knots per axis, each method evaluated at a hundred thousand
random points. Left, the largest error as the grid is refined; right, the time to construct
and to evaluate at the hundred thousand points against that error, which is the cost of a
given accuracy when the interpolant is used in earnest.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The three-dimensional study"
ns3 = [11, 21, 41, 81]
tp3 = testpoints(3, 100_000)
res3 = Dict()                                             # (name, n) => (time to construct and evaluate, error)
for n in ns3
    ax = axes_nd(3, n); v = values_nd(3, n)
    for (name, m) in methods_nd
        itp = m(ax, v)
        res3[(name, n)] = (time = (@b $m($ax, $v)).time + (@b evalpts($itp, $(tp3.P))).time,
                           err  = maximum(abs.(evalpts(itp, tp3.P) .- tp3.exact)))
    end
end

hs3 = 2 ./ (ns3 .- 1)
fig = Figure(size = (800, 520))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true, xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error")
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xlabel = "time to construct and evaluate [s]")
linkyaxes!(ax1, ax2)
for (name, _) in methods_nd
    scatterlines!(ax1, hs3, [res3[(name, n)].err for n in ns3]; markersize = 8, label = name)
    scatterlines!(ax2, [res3[(name, n)].time for n in ns3], [res3[(name, n)].err for n in ns3]; markersize = 8)
end
Legend(fig[2, 1:2], ax1; orientation = :horizontal, nbanks = 2)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| largest error | ", join(("$(n)³" for n in ns3), " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(ns3))
for (name, _) in methods_nd
    println("| ", name, " | ", join((@sprintf("%.1e", res3[(name, n)].err) for n in ns3), " | "), " |")
end
println()
println("| time to construct and evaluate | ", join(("$(n)³" for n in ns3), " | "), " |")
println("|:--|", "--:|"^length(ns3))
for (name, _) in methods_nd
    println("| ", name, " | ", join((fmt(res3[(name, n)].time) for n in ns3), " | "), " |")
end
```

The time is dominated by the hundred thousand evaluations, so the right panel is the cost per
point against the order. On the coarsest grid the cubic B-spline is the most accurate method
per millisecond. From the next grid on, the picture inverts: `:a4`, `:b5` and `:b7` reach
accuracies on 21³ and 41³ that the cubic does not reach on 81³, in a fraction of the time it
takes there, because the cost per point grows with the stencil only once while the error falls
with the order at every refinement. For an accuracy of one part in ten thousand or better in
three dimensions, the kernels are the faster route; for a rough interpolant, the splines are.

## Lazy construction

An eager interpolant copies the data into an array padded with ghost values along every axis,
and the ghost values are the construction cost; a lazy one stores the data as they are and
forms the ghost values it needs when a point near the boundary is evaluated. The same ghost
values, so the two agree to rounding everywhere; the difference is where the work is done.
Three grids with `:b7`, eager against lazy construction time, and which of the two the
default chooses:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Eager against lazy construction"
cases = [(3, 100), (4, 30), (5, 12)]
lz = map(cases) do (N, n)
    ax = axes_nd(N, n); v = values_nd(N, n)
    (N = N, n = n,
     eager = (@b convolution_interpolation($ax, $v; kernel = :b7, lazy = false)).time,
     lazy  = (@b convolution_interpolation($ax, $v; kernel = :b7, lazy = true)).time,
     default = convolution_interpolation(ax, v; kernel = :b7).itp.lazy isa Val{true} ? "lazy" : "eager")
end;
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| grid | eager | lazy | speedup | default |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|")
for c in lz
    @printf("| %dD %d%s | %s | %s | %.0f× | %s |\n", c.N, c.n, ("", "", "³", "⁴", "⁵")[c.N], fmt(c.eager), fmt(c.lazy), c.eager / c.lazy, c.default)
end
```

Lazy construction costs microseconds whatever the grid, since nothing is copied, while eager
construction grows with the number of ghost values, which grows with the dimension and the
kernel's width. The default, `lazy = nothing`, builds eagerly until eager construction would
exceed either of two limits — $2^{27}$ values in the padded array, which is a gigabyte in
`Float64`, or $2^{24}$ ghost values, which is about a second of construction — and lazily
beyond them, so the three grids here are built eagerly by default, and a user who constructs
many interpolants or evaluates few points sets `lazy = true` and pays nothing at construction.
Evaluation in the interior is the same in both modes; near the boundary a lazy interpolant
computes its ghost values on the fly, so eager is the faster choice when boundary cells are
evaluated often.

## Choosing a kernel in many dimensions

- The default kernel follows the dimension for this reason: `:b7` in one and two dimensions,
  `:b5` in three, `:a4` in four and five, `:a3` from six — the widest kernel whose stencil is
  still cheap at that dimension.
- Where more accuracy is wanted than the default gives, a wider kernel buys it at the
  stencil's $w^N$ per evaluation, which the tables above put in numbers; where speed is
  wanted, `:a3` has the cubic B-spline's stencil and `:a1` the cheapest.
- Build large grids lazily; the default does so beyond its limits, and `lazy = true` always
  works.
- A grid uniform along some axes and nonuniform along others, or with different kernels per
  axis, costs each axis its own kernel's width and no more; the
  [concept page](../../concepts/interpolation.qmd) has the per-axis keywords.
